table.text: Participants completed the survey anonymously on an iPad.
table.header: Data source and study participants:

table.text: Participants were classified as overweight if the BMI was ≥ 85th percentile and < 95th percentile for age (if under 20 years) or if the BMI was ≥ 25 and < 30 kg/m2 (if 20 years of age and older), and with obesity if the BMI was ≥ 95th percentile for age (if under 20 years) or if the BMI was ≥ 30 kg/m2 (if aged 20 years and older). 20, 21 We surveyed young women regarding their overall outlook on life and adherence to cardiovascular health recommendations.

table.header: Measures and Study Design:

table.text: 331 participants completed the survey, and their characteristics are summarized in Table 1 Overall Outlook on life and influential factors Young women rated their overall outlook on life as excellent (8%, N=26), very good (27%, N=82), good (35%, N=107), fair (26%, N=81), or poor (4%, N=11).

table.header: Results:

table.text: Our observations align with prior findings indicating an association between optimism and cardiovascular health trajectory in adult studies, suggesting a cardioprotective role of optimism detectable at an earlier age than previously described. 10, [14] [15] [16] While this association was slightly attenuated by socio-economic indicators, the relationship in this study appears mediated by discrete factors in the lived environment that were more proximally influential, likely reflecting our participants' developmental stage. 16 This mediating effect may be especially pronounced among young women of color, possibly reflecting contextual constraints that limit the extent to which positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants completed the survey anonymously on an iPad.

> Participants were classified as overweight if the BMI was ≥ 85th percentile and < 95th percentile for age (if under 20 years) or if the BMI was ≥ 25 and < 30 kg/m2 (if 20 years of age and older), and with obesity if the BMI was ≥ 95th percentile for age (if under 20 years) or if the BMI was ≥ 30 kg/m2 (if aged 20 years and older). 20, 21 We surveyed young women regarding their overall outlook on life and adherence to cardiovascular health recommendations.

> 331 participants completed the survey, and their characteristics are summarized in Table 1 Overall Outlook on life and influential factors Young women rated their overall outlook on life as excellent (8%, N=26), very good (27%, N=82), good (35%, N=107), fair (26%, N=81), or poor (4%, N=11).

> Our observations align with prior findings indicating an association between optimism and cardiovascular health trajectory in adult studies, suggesting a cardioprotective role of optimism detectable at an earlier age than previously described. 10, [14] [15] [16] While this association was slightly attenuated by socio-economic indicators, the relationship in this study appears mediated by discrete factors in the lived environment that were more proximally influential, likely reflecting our participants' developmental stage. 16 This mediating effect may be especially pronounced among young women of color, possibly reflecting contextual constraints that limit the extent to which positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes.

Ethics approval statement:

> The Hospital Institutional Review Board approved this study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: While these findings are encouraging and suggest new avenues in cardiovascular prevention strategies, we acknowledge several limitations in our study. A primary limitation is the crosssectional design, which makes our findings observational and prevents establishing a causal relationship between overall outlook on life and cardiovascular health behaviors. Although caregiver education level is widely used to assess the relationship between socioeconomic circumstances and cardiovascular disease outcomes, our reliance on it as a proxy for socioeconomic status limited our ability to fully characterize socioeconomic influences on this relationship. 19 Additionally, our reliance on self-reported data introduces potential recall and social desirability biases, particularly for sensitive items such as adherence to healthy eating or sleep habits. Furthermore, although our sample was adequately powered to detect the observed associations, it may not fully represent the broader population of young women, limiting generalizability. Lastly, our data were collected from a 2017-2018 AHA Women's Health Survey dataset for young women; given evolving mental health trends among adolescents in subsequent years, including during the COVID-19 pandemic, more contemporary data may better capture current patterns in outlook on life and cardiovascular health behaviors.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}

"In this analysis, compared to women under the age of 18 (27%; N=91), young women aged 18 years and older (63%; N=209) were more likely to report a higher impact of outlook on life on their likelihood of developing (OR=1.45; 95% CI [1.17, 1.80]; P<0.01).", 
"Similarly, there were no statistical differences between Hispanic and non-Hispanic young women on the impact of outlook on life on developing or managing serious illness (P>0.20) compared to other races.",
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p>0.1", "P = 0.09", "P = 0.60", "P>0.20" ), Sentence = c("Associations with race, ethnicity, or BMI were nonsignificant (p>0.1).", "Age differences in the impact of outlook on life on managing serious illness, such as heart disease, were nonsignificant (P = 0.09).", "Differences between racial groups in the impact of outlook on life on successfully managing a serious illness like heart disease were nonsignificant (P = 0.60).", "Similarly, there were no statistical differences between Hispanic and non-Hispanic young women on the impact of outlook on life on developing or managing serious illness (P>0.20) compared to other races." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

live_data_statements: Participants completed the survey anonymously on an iPad.

Participants were classified as overweight if the BMI was ≥ 85th percentile and < 95th percentile for age (if under 20 years) or if the BMI was ≥ 25 and < 30 kg/m2 (if 20 years of age and older), and with obesity if the BMI was ≥ 95th percentile for age (if under 20 years) or if the BMI was ≥ 30 kg/m2 (if aged 20 years and older). 20, 21 We surveyed young women regarding their overall outlook on life and adherence to cardiovascular health recommendations.

331 participants completed the survey, and their characteristics are summarized in Table 1 Overall Outlook on life and influential factors Young women rated their overall outlook on life as excellent (8%, N=26), very good (27%, N=82), good (35%, N=107), fair (26%, N=81), or poor (4%, N=11).

Our observations align with prior findings indicating an association between optimism and cardiovascular health trajectory in adult studies, suggesting a cardioprotective role of optimism detectable at an earlier age than previously described. 10, [14] [15] [16] While this association was slightly attenuated by socio-economic indicators, the relationship in this study appears mediated by discrete factors in the lived environment that were more proximally influential, likely reflecting our participants' developmental stage. 16 This mediating effect may be especially pronounced among young women of color, possibly reflecting contextual constraints that limit the extent to which positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes.
